sections.overview: Apistogramma steindachneri is a comparatively large dwarf cichlid from the Guiana region of northeastern South America. Charles Tate Regan described it in 1908 as Heterogramma steindachneri, using specimens from Georgetown on Guyana’s Demerara River.
sections.identification: The diagnostic pattern combines a narrow dark side band, a triangular black spot centered on that band, and a separate round spot at the tail base. It lacks the abdominal stripes found in some look-alikes, while adult males develop longer dorsal rays and a squared or lyre-shaped tail; females retain a rounder tail. FishBase lists males or unsexed fish to 65 mm standard length and females to 70 mm total length. The Swedish register gives 10 cm without specifying the measure; no reliable mass, body width or height was found.
sections.habitat: Records span the Essequibo, Demerara and Mahaica drainages of Guyana and rivers from the Marowijne to the Corantijn in Suriname. It uses slower tributaries and streams with leaf litter and submerged wood, and a similar Cuyuni-basin form in Venezuela remains taxonomically uncertain.
sections.diet: No direct stomach-content study was located in the sources consulted. FishBase gives a trophic estimate derived from related species, so small invertebrates are a plausible dwarf-cichlid diet, not a measured species-specific menu.
sections.behavior: Adult males may defend a harem of several females and multiple nesting sites; females tend the cave brood while the larger males guard the territory.
sections.reproduction: Females deposit roughly 60–120 eggs on the ceiling of a cave, and the female tends the eggs and larvae. The male’s role is mainly territorial, guarding the nesting sites used by the females in his harem.
sections.ecology: This species belongs to the steindachneri lineage, whose members share a conspicuous flank spot; the spot’s position on the lateral band helps identify true A. steindachneri. It is distinct from A. staecki, a similarly sized member of the same broad lineage found far to the southwest in Bolivia and Brazil.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists Apistogramma steindachneri as Least Concern, assessed on 29 October 2020. This category applies to the named species; it does not settle whether the Venezuelan Cuyuni form is part of the same species.
